Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3301 : Bioprocess Instrumentation and Control { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I
Introduction: Bioprocess – Historical background Stages of bioprocessing Bioreactors – types and design considerations Principles of measurements Significance of process control and Classification of process control instruments.
Module II
Sensors: Temperature, pH, Dissolved Oxygen, Level, Foam, Flow rate, Humidity, Density, Viscosity, Turbidity, Pressure, Biosensors.
Module III
Instruments: Chromatography: Fundamental Principles, Types and Instrumentation, High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) Spectroscopy: Fundamental Principles, Types and Instrumentation Off-gas analysers Valves and Actuators.
Module IV:
Bioprocess Control: Components of a control system Development of block diagram for a bioprocess control system Modelling of Process Dynamics: First principle models, Empirical and Grey Box models, first and second-order dynamical systems and their response Open and closed-loop control systems Controllers: Proportional (P), ON/OFF, Proportional-Integral (PI), Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controllers.

Course Objective

1 .

To become familiar with various methods of bioprocess control and instrumentation.
2 .

To understand the basic principles of sensors and actuators.
3 .

To learn techniques of chromatography and spectroscopy in bioprocess engineering.
4 .

To understand classical approaches for controlling the processes.

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of the course, the students will be able to:
CO1: Explain the significance of bioreactor design, instrumentation and control in development of optimal bioprocesses.
CO2: Identify and understand the principle behind various sensors and instruments for measurement of important process parameters.
CO3: Explain the fundamental principles of chromatography and spectroscopy.
CO4: Describe the dynamic behaviour of bioprocesses in the bioreactor.
CO5: Understand process control strategies using classical approaches.

1 .

RS Khandpur, Handbook of analytical instruments, McGraw Hill

2 .

Donald R. Coughanowr, Steven E. LeBlanc, Process Systems Analysis and Control, McGraw Hill

6445.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6234 : Pre-Stressed Concrete { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Basics of Prestressing (8 hours)
Introduction, Prestressing systems: Pre-tensioning, Post-Tensioning, Anchorage systems, Chemical Prestressing, Electro-thermal prestressing, Wire, Bar, strand, tendon, IS code provisions for tensile strength vs diameter, cold drawing of steel,
Concenctric tendon: Relation between prestressing force during jacking and prestressing force after concrete has set, hydrogen embrittlement, clear cover provisions, IS code provisions for limits on prestressing tensile force in bars
Analysis of flexure: Force transfer for eccentric sections, Concept of pressure line, Load balancing concept

Module 2 :

Module II: Losses of Prestress (7 hours)
Loss of Prestress: Elastic deformation of concrete, Friction, wobbling effect, Anchorage slip, creep in concrete, Creep of concrete, stress relaxation, concrete shrinkage
Module 3 :

Module III: Analysis of flexure, Deflections, Magnel’s Approach (13 hours)
Analysis of flexure: Basic concepts, Simplified codal procedure for analysis of flexure,British Code and American Codes for analysis of flexure
Deflection of uncracked members: Short Term and Long Term
Deflection of cracked members: Short Term, Limits on deflection in Code, British Code BS EN 1992-1-1
Magnel’s Approach: Stresses in steel in prestressed concrete, service load design basics Stress range approach for flexure design and Magnel's approach

Module 4 :

Module IV: Shear, Bond, Anchorage (4 hours)
Shear stress in prestressed beams: Basics, examples Shear stress resistance, modes of failure Design for shear in uncracked and cracked section Design for torsion
Bond: Transmission Length, Bond stress, Transverse tensile stress, End zone reinforcement, Flexural bond stress,
Anchorage stresses in end zone: Using Magnel's method and Guoyon's method, IS codal provisions.
Module 5 :

Module V: Statically Indeterminate Analysis (4 hours)
Statically indeterminate analysis in continuous prestressed beams: Primary moment, secondary moment, moment distribution method, C-line, Linear transformation, concordant cable

Course Objective

1 .

Students will attain a solid mastery of the fundamental principles of prestressing.
2 .

Students will cultivate a high level of proficiency in the analysis and design of prestressed concrete elements.
3 .

Students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of the essential code provisions important for the design of prestressed members.
4 .

Students will proficiently apply advanced statically indeterminate analysis techniques to the design of prestressed structures.

Course Outcome

1 .

Students will demonstrate a thorough understanding of the fundamentals of prestressed concrete design.
2 .

Students will accurately determine prestress losses

3 .

Students will analyze and design girders for flexure, shear, and torsion, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the applicable codal provisions.

4 .

Students will accurately calculate deflections as part of their design evaluations.
5 .

Students will effectively perform statically indeterminate analyses of prestressed members.

Essential Reading

1 .

N. Rajagopalan, Prestressed concrete, Narosa

2 .

N. Krishnaraju, Prestressed concrete, Tata McGraw-Hill

Supplementary Reading

1 .

T. Y. Lin and N. H. Burns, Design of Prestressed concrete structures, John Willey & Sons

2 .

A.E. Naaman, Prestressed Concrete Analysis and Design – Fundamentals, CBS

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CY2201 : Principles of Inorganic Chemistry { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Atomic Structure: de-Broglie matter waves, Uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation, quantum numbers and its significance, Radial and angular wave functions, Radial and angular distribution curves, shape of s, p, d orbitals, Angular and radial nodes, sign of orbitals. Pauli’s exclusion principle, Hund’s rule of maximum multiplicity, Aufbau’s principle and its limitations, Variation of orbital energy with atomic number. [8 hours]
Module 2: Periodicity of Elements: Effective nuclear charge, shielding or screening effect, Slater rules, variation of effective nuclear charge in periodic table. Atomic radii (van der Waals), Ionic and crystal radii, Covalent radii (octahedral and tetrahedral), Ionization energy and its applications. Electron affinity, Electronegativity, Pauling’s and Mulliken’s electronegativity scales. [8 hours]
Module 3: Chemical Bonding: Ionic bond: types of ions, size effects, radius ratio rule and its limitations. Packing of ions in crystals. Structure of NaCl, CsCl, ZnS, TiO2, CdI2. Expression for lattice energy. Born equation, polarizability, Fajan’s rule, and its applications. Covalent bonds: Lewis theory, Resonance, VBT, quantum mechanical approach to hybridization, directional characteristics, deduction of geometry by VSEPR method, Bent’s Rule, Qualitative treatment of MO theory applied to homo (N2 vs O2) and hetero (HF, CO, NO) diatomic molecules. [8 hours]
Module 4: Coordination Chemistry: Ligands, coordination numbers, coordination sphere, Nomenclature, Werner’s theory, EAN, Chelates, isomerism in coordination compounds, Valence Bond theory, Crystal Field Theory, octahedral, tetrahedral and square planner complexes, calculation of CFSE in octahedral and tetrahedral geometry. [8 hours]
Module 5: Bioinorganic Chemistry: Essential metal ions, Biological ligands for metal ions, Metal ions specificity, O2 storage/transport: Myoglobin/Hemoglobin. [3 hours]

Course Objective

1 .

Students would be able to relate the fundamental principles of matter, atomic theory and chemical bonding with aspects of basic science and technology.
2 .

Gives an idea about the properties and reactivities of elements of periodic table
3 .

Provides basic understanding about the reactivities of common inorganic compounds

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Students would be able to relate the fundamental principles of matter, atomic theory and chemical bonding with aspects of basic science and technology.
CO2: Gives an idea about the properties and reactivities of elements of periodic table.
CO3: Provides basic understanding about the reactivities of common inorganic compounds.

Essential Reading

1 .

Huheey, Keiter and Keiter, , Inorganic chemistry Principle, structure and reactivity. 4th edition., Pearson

2 .

D. F. Shriver, P. W. Atkins and C. H. Langford, Inorganic Chemistry, Oxford University Press

Supplementary Reading

1 .

G. L. Miessler and D. A. Tarr, Inorganic Chemistry, Pearson

2 .

M. Chanda, Structure and Chemical bond, Tata McGraw Hill

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA1512 : Evolution of Architecture - II { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I (5 hrs) / Pre-historic period (till 4th cent. BCE): Indus-Saraswati River valley civilization and its architecture principles of architecture and town planning adopted in Vedic settlements.
Module-II (8 hrs) / 4th cent. BCE till 5th cent. CE: Introduction to religious architecture of the Buddhists rock-cut architecture, building types and other architectural features (rock-cut cave, stupa, vihara, chaitya griha, etc.) Assignment: Explore evolution of rock-cut cave temples using physical models.
Module-III (11 hrs) / 5th till 13th cent. CE: Introduction to Hindu temple architecture evolution of temple form in both north and south of Vindhyas classification of temples north of Vindhyas into Latina, Shekhari, and Bhumija and hybrid forms (i.e., Vesara) evolution of temples north of Vindhyas by the Guptas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and their feudatories (i.e., Solankis, Paramars, Kacchapagathas, Chandelas) and in Kalinga evolution of temples south of Vindhyas under Pallavas, Cholas, Chalukyas, Pandyas, and Hoysalas development of temple towns in south of Vindhyas Assignment: Explore the evolution of temple forms using physical models Compare temple forms developed in north and south of Vindhyas (poster).
Module-IV (12 hrs) / 13th till 18th cent. CE: Introduction to the architecture of mosques and tombs in the Islamic World, and arcuated structural systems (arches, squinches, and domes) evolution of architectural forms during Sultanate period in Delhi regional influences in provinces north of Vindhyas, i.e., Gujarat, Bengal, Jaunpur, and Malwa regional influences in provinces south of Vindhyas, i.e., by Bahamanis in Gulbarga and Bidar and later by Adil Shahis and Qutb Shahis in Bijapur and Golconda, respectively Hindu experiments (temples, palaces, forts, and others) in Vijayanagara, Kerala Rajputs in Chittorgarh, Gwalior and Orccha, etc. key elements of Mughal architecture (amalgamation of Persian and indigenous traditions) Review of colonial architecture in Indian subcontinent – both in colonies of the Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British in India, and Princely States of India Assignment: Explore the architecture of arcuated forms using physical models Identify architectural elements signifying assimilation of indigenously developed and imported architectural traditions.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the evolution of architecture in India since the Indus-Saraswati River valley civilization till Mughal Empire (i.e., 18th cent. CE).
2 .

To identify the factors influencing architectural development of a region, such as temporal changes in political patronage, socio-cultural institutions, semiotics, assimilation of indigenous and imported architectural systems, and others.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. An ability to identify and appreciate the diversity in architectural practices developed in a region over a period.
2. An ability to understand that architecture of any region is shaped by a multitude of factors ranging from availability of material resources to structures of socio-cultural and political order.
3. An ability to understand that architecture of any region is ever evolving, subject to changes in local and/or global orders and use patterns.

Essential Reading

Tadgell, C., The history of architecture in India, Phaidon , 1994

2 .

Grover, S., The Architecture of India (Buddhist & Hindu, Islamic), Vikas Publishing House , 1980

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Brown, P., Indian Architecture (Vol. I & II), Taraporevala and Sons , 1956

2 .

Kramrisch, S., The Hindu Temple, Vol. I and II, MLBD Publishers , 1976

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA4416 : Cities and Climate Change { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I- Cities, Urbanization, and the Challenge of Climate Change:
Urbanization and climate change, evidence of climate change: implications for urban centres, the framework for exploring the linkages between urban areas and climate change, the United Nations Framework Convention on climate change, the Kyoto Protocol, other climate change arrangements, the potential of the international climate change framework for local action.
Module II- Effects of climate change on cities:
The impacts of climate change upon urban areas, impacts upon physical infrastructure, economic impacts, public health impacts, social impacts, displacement and forced migration, identifying cities vulnerable to climate change, concluding remarks and lessons for policy.
Assignment(s): Exercises on documenting the impact of climate on cities
Module III- Cities as contributors to climate change:
The contribution of urban areas to climate change, measuring greenhouse gas emissions, the sources of greenhouse gas emissions, the scale of urban emissions, factors influencing emissions.
Assignment(s): Exercises on documentation of the impact of the city on climate change
Module IV- Integrating climate change mitigation in urban planning:
Climate change mitigation responses in urban areas, responses to climate change mitigation in urban areas, urban governance for climate change mitigation, opportunities, and constraints,
Assignment(s): Exercises on mitigation strategies for climate change
Module V- Urban climate change adaptation in practice:
Climate change adaptation responses in urban areas, understanding adaptation, household, and community responses to the impacts of climate change, local government responses to the impacts of climate change, towards effective city-based climate change adaptation strategies, financing adaptation, challenges to adaptation, concluding remarks and lessons for policy.
Assignment(s): Exercises on adaption strategies for climate change
Module VI- Overview of major initiatives related to climate change and cities:
Key findings and their implications, addressing urban GHG emissions and vulnerabilities: challenges, constraints and opportunities, adaptation and mitigation: relationships with urban development and policy, future policy directions.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand how cities are affected by climate change and how cities are contributing to climate change.
2 .

To understand how climate change adaptation and mitigation can be integrated in city planning.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Ability to describe the transformative role that cities can play in achieving green and climate resilient development.
2. Ability to explain how urban areas are affected by, and contribute to, climate change.
3. Ability to identify mitigation measures suitable for urban areas.
4. Ability to explain how climate change adaptation can be considered in urban planning.

Essential Reading

1 .

UN-Habitat, Planning for Climate Change, UN-Habitat , 2014

2 .

United Nations Human Settlements Programme, Cities And Climate Change Global Report on Human Settlements, Earthscan , 2011

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Rosenzweig, C., Solecki, W. D., Hammer, S. A., & Mehrotra, S., Climate Change and Cities: First Assessment Report of the Urban Climate Change Research Network, Cambridge University Press , 2011

2 .

Bulkeley, H., Cities and Climate Change, Routledge , 2013, ISBN: 9780415597050
